examples.name: Resources barrier
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests employees lack resources, support, or clarity about how to remove blockers.
recommended_candidate_titles: Develop a Support Network for Your Team
examples.selection_note: Start with a concrete barrier-finding or support-network action before broader learning resources.
examples.act_application: Acknowledge blockers in the results, collaborate on the most important barrier, and take one support-network step before the next check-in.
examples.why_action_matters: Use the action-taking evidence to reinforce that visible action matters and that managers should focus on one high-impact blocker rather than trying to fix everything.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, frame this as a practical roadblock-removal story: survey signal, team barrier, one support action, and check-in cadence.

examples.name: Inclusion concern
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests team members may not feel heard, included, or able to contribute fully.
recommended_candidate_titles: Be Inclusive by Changing Communication Patterns
Seek Diverse Perspectives When Adding New Team Members
examples.selection_note: Prefer behavior and communication-pattern actions over generic resources.
examples.act_application: Acknowledge where people do not feel heard, collaborate on one inclusion behavior to try, and check whether participation changes.
examples.why_action_matters: Use psychological-safety evidence when the inclusion issue is about voice, belonging, or fear of speaking up; otherwise use ACT to emphasize shared ownership and one small behavior shift.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, show the manager conversation arc: acknowledge participation gaps, collaborate on one inclusive behavior, and revisit whether more voices are showing up.

examples.name: Manager support gap
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests the manager needs to provide clearer support, advocacy, communication, or access to help.
recommended_candidate_titles: Bridge Communication Between Senior Leaders and Your Team
Build trust and inclusive team communication
examples.selection_note: Choose based on whether the evidence points to missing support resources, communication flow, or trust.
examples.act_application: Use the team conversation to clarify what support means, pick one visible support action, and revisit it in a recurring team rhythm.
examples.why_action_matters: Use the action-taking evidence to make the case that manager follow-through and recurring conversations help employees see feedback is valued.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, position the manager as coach/facilitator: clarify support needs, choose one visible support behavior, and make progress visible.

examples.name: Leadership confidence
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests employees need better context about senior leadership decisions and company direction.
recommended_candidate_titles: Be a Link Between Senior Leaders and Your Team
Share how the company addresses your team's needs
examples.selection_note: Favor actions that bridge leadership decisions to team concerns.
examples.act_application: Acknowledge uncertainty about leadership decisions, collaborate on the questions the team needs answered, and take one communication step.
examples.why_action_matters: Use the action-taking evidence that action planning is associated with confidence in leadership; frame the action as connecting team concerns to leadership context.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, present a leadership-confidence story: decision context, team questions, manager-as-connector action, and follow-up rhythm.

examples.name: Feedback acceptance
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests the leader needs to visibly value input and respond constructively to feedback.
recommended_candidate_titles: Show Your Team That You Value Their Input
examples.selection_note: Start with visible feedback/listening behavior; use self-assessment when the leader needs reflection before team action.
examples.act_application: Acknowledge the feedback, collaborate with the team on one behavior to improve, and take one visible follow-up action.
examples.why_action_matters: Use ACT and psychological-safety context to reinforce that feedback only becomes safer when managers visibly listen, regulate defensiveness, and follow through.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, emphasize the visible behavior change: feedback received, manager response habit, and one follow-up action.

examples.name: Acceptance and belonging
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests people need a more inclusive environment where difference and belonging are supported.
examples.selection_note: This question has a narrow candidate set; use the matched action record directly.
examples.act_application: Use ACT to help the team define what acceptance looks like and pick one inclusion practice to try.
examples.why_action_matters: Use psychological-safety context to explain why acceptance and belonging matter for safe participation, learning, and healthy team dynamics.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, package as an inclusion conversation: what acceptance means here, one practice to try, and how the team will check whether it helped.

examples.name: Voice and psychological safety
examples.evidence_pattern: Low score suggests people may not feel safe raising concerns, asking questions, or speaking up about risks and mistakes.
recommended_candidate_titles: Build psychological safety for your team
Questions to Ask that can Lead to Action
examples.selection_note: Prefer trust-building and conversation records; use the psychological safety source to frame manager behaviors like checking reactivity, listening without agenda, and modeling vulnerability.
examples.act_application: Acknowledge that speaking up may not feel safe, collaborate on what would make voice easier, and take one visible manager behavior step before the next check-in.
examples.why_action_matters: Use the psychological-safety evidence directly: lower psychological safety is associated with higher intent to quit and lower motivation; the video also links psychological safety with lower turnover and stress and higher productivity.
examples.presentation_packaging: If preparing slides, use the psychological-safety facts as the evidence slide, then show the three manager behaviors: check reactivity, listen without agenda, and model vulnerability.
